job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**Drafting and enforcement issues in S. 2817 (as amended October 6)**

1. **§2(1)(A), volume threshold:** The 10,000-ton test applies per vessel, not per company or project. An operator could split activity across several vessels, each below the line, and fall outside the definition.

2. **§2(1)(A), "recovery" and tonnage:** Neither term is defined. The bill doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry weight, or whether it's measured before or after sediment is separated, so a company could contest any measurement.

3. **§2(1)(A), "commercial":** The defined term uses "commercial," but the test is purely volume-based. Commercially motivated activity below 10,000 tons, such as a sizable test collection, falls outside the definition.

4. **§2(1)(B), "Secretary":** The subparagraph refers to "the Secretary" without specifying which one. Section 6 uses "Secretary of State," so the bill never identifies the official who makes the determinations that matter most.

5. **§2(1)(B), "comparable" risk standard:** This catch-all has no criteria, procedure, notice, or record requirement. Determinations could be made quietly, and they would be open to challenge as arbitrary and capricious.

6. **§2(2), "U.S. person":** Limiting this to citizens and state-chartered corporations excludes LLCs, partnerships, and foreign-organized subsidiaries of U.S. companies. A company could conduct operations through an offshore entity that falls outside §3(a)'s "any U.S. person anywhere" reach.

7. **§3(a), "engage in":** This phrase is undefined. It's unclear whether it covers financing, insurance, equipment supply, chartering, technology licensing, or management from U.S. offices.

8. **§3(a), scope of the prohibition:** The ban covers only recovery. It doesn't address processing, transport, sale, or import of nodules or metals, so recovered material could still enter U.S. supply chains.

9. **§3(a), foreign activity:** The bill doesn't reach foreign persons operating abroad, and it doesn't address mining in the Area under International Seabed Authority contracts, including sponsorship arrangements through foreign states.

10. **§2(3) and §4, vessel gap:** The reporting and registration duties attach only to "covered vessels" (over 5,000 gross tons). A vessel under that size could exceed the 10,000-ton activity threshold without ever being registered or reporting.

11. **§2(3) and §4, undefined terms:** "Equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources" and "operator" are both undefined. Support vessels, converted vessels, and chartered vessels could fall outside the registration duty.

12. **§3(b), existing-operations exemption:** "Exploration license" is undefined and isn't tied to any existing federal permit regime. Read literally, "mining conducted under" such a license could cover full commercial recovery, and the exemption has no volume, area, or end-date limit.

13. **§3(b), grandfathered licenses:** The bill doesn't restrict transfer, assignment, renewal, expansion, or new vessels or areas under a pre-enactment license. It's also unclear whether a renewal issued after enactment counts as "issued before the date of enactment."

14. **§3(c), environmental assessment carve-out:** "Activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment" has no definition, volume cap, duration limit, approval requirement, or reporting duty. A commercial-scale operation could be labeled assessment, and the "purpose" standard would be hard for regulators to disprove.

15. **§4(a), registration:** The bill sets no registration deadline, specifies no content, and defines no consequence for failing to register.

16. **§4(b), quarterly reports:** The reports have no required content (tonnage, location, depth, discharges, sampling), no verification or audit provision, no public disclosure requirement, and no deadline. A narrative "description" could technically satisfy the duty.

17. **§4 and §5, enforcement gap:** Section 5 penalizes only violations of §3. Failing to register, failing to file reports, or certifying false reports carries no civil or criminal penalty, which leaves the monitoring regime effectively unenforceable.

18. **Missing enforcement machinery:** The bill gives no agency inspection, subpoena, records-retention, or vessel-detention authority, names no agency to bring civil penalty actions, and sets no statute of limitations. Without these, the Act has no practical way to detect or prove violations.

19. **§5(a), civil penalty mechanics:** "Each day on which the violation occurs" is undefined for continuing activity, and the bill sets no penalty factors. It also doesn't say whether penalties are assessed administratively or in court, or whether vessels are liable in rem.

20. **§5(a) and §8, effective-date conflict:** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §3 doesn't take effect until 180 days later. This creates an argument about when liability begins and invites litigation over the timing.

21. **§5(b), criminal penalty:** "Willfully" is undefined, and the bill doesn't specify whether corporate officers are personally liable. It also doesn't reach aiding, abetting, conspiracy, or financing, and it sets no corporate fine amount beyond the general Title 18 reference.

22. **§6, international agreement:** "Shall seek to negotiate" creates no obligation to reach an agreement, and it sets no consequence or reporting requirement if negotiations fail. The "equivalent" standard is also vague.

23. **§7(a) and §7(b), direct conflict:** Subsection (a) keeps the prohibition in place until Congress lifts it by joint resolution, while subsection (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years. A court would have to choose between them, and opponents could argue the protection is time-limited.

24. **§7(a), "serious harm" and review trigger:** "Serious harm" is undefined, the NASEM report has no deadline or defined scope, and the bill doesn't say how the joint resolution interacts with presentment and veto.

25. **Missing interaction clause:** The bill doesn't say whether it supersedes, amends, or coexists with the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (1980) and existing NOAA licenses and permits. That silence invites arguments that permits issued under the 1980 Act still authorize activity. Counsel should confirm the current statutory framework before relying on this point.

26. **Missing general provisions:** The bill has no severability clause, no judicial review or citizen-suit provision, and no rulemaking authority. Without a citizen-suit provision, enforcement depends entirely on agency discretion.

**For the markup, I'd prioritize:**
- **§7(a)/(b) conflict** (#23): an easy fix that exposes the bill's core protection to a time limit.
- **§4/§5 enforcement gap** (#17) and **missing enforcement machinery** (#18): these make the reporting regime unenforceable.
- **§3(b) grandfathering** (#12, #13) and **§3(c) assessment carve-out** (#14): these are the broadest paths for existing operations to continue.
- **Per-vessel threshold and vessel gap** (#1, #10): these are the easiest structural routes around the prohibition.

This analysis is based only on the bill text you provided. Before the markup, have counsel check it against the official text and any CRS analysis, confirm the current DSHMRA provisions, and verify the October 6 manager's amendment language.
